items.title: Migrating our Messages API to Rust
items.content:
01
Why migrate?
Many problems have a
generator–verifier
gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing
proofs
in mathematics or
migrating
large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.
But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that
fall outside the test suite
, and it’s hard to write
a definition of “correct” that covers everything
. Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it.
We ran into this problem when we migrated our
Messages API
from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged.
In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development.
Why migrate?
We built the Messages API in 2023 and wrote it in Python, which was widely used internally for much of our research code. At first, it was simple. The Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote. (One engineer at the time called it “basically a request forwarder.”) But as the Messages API became more capable and deeply integrated with our codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries that were owned by our research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. If we ever wanted to move to another language, it would mean building logging, metrics, and tools all over again.
This calculus gradually began to change. By late 2025, every Messages API request had to be validated, converted into the prompt, tokenized, and screened by our safety classifiers. As each reply arrived, the stream of tokens had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls, and Python added overhead to every one of those steps each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed its work to the next task. Traffic eventually grew far beyond what the initial Python service was built for (Figure 1), and we quickly needed to find a way to make the service much more efficient.
The monthly average of API requests per day on our own platform, including our own use.
Incremental or all at once?
Full rewrites of large production systems are often approached cautiously, for at least two reasons. First, there is no guarantee that test suites cover 100% of production code behavior, and rewriting it is risky. Second, the sheer effort required often makes such work intractable. (In 2024, after one of our engineers suggested migrating to Go or Rust, another temporarily settled the question: “
We are not rewriting the API in go or rust!
”)
The standard advice if you’re looking for performance gains is thus to rewrite only the parts that are slowing the system down, so that’s where we started. In Rust, we rewrote the code that parses a model’s output and called it from Python. This reduced the API’s CPU usage by about 8% to 10%. However, incremental solutions often incur added complexity, and it’s important to make sure that incremental improvements justify those costs. In our case, the gains didn’t justify the added complexity. Each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times (Figure 2), creating new sources of overhead.
After the incremental rewrite, each token of a reply crossed between Python and Rust three times.
As Claude became increasingly capable, we began to question whether the usual reasons to avoid a full migration still held. The effort required to undertake the project was dropping fast: by May 2026, Claude was writing
more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged
. We wondered if Claude could now help us write code that would empirically capture every behavior and fix in the production system. But the question became: how could we verify that the behavior of our migration was correct? Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck.
How we verified the migration
General approaches
To verify the migration, we first needed to define what “correct” meant. You can do this in a few ways (Figure 3). If you’re lucky, you can simply write a rule. A
theorem in mathematics
is a precise statement, and a proof assistant (like Lean) can check each step of a proof against a fixed set of rules. Other times—and more frequently in software engineering—you define “correct” with a set of examples, like tests. For instance, when
Bun moved
from Zig to Rust, its test suite was written in TypeScript, so the same tests could judge both versions. In our case, neither approach was sufficient, so we used the existing system as an oracle to test parity during the migration. In this case, our existing system (the Messages API) kept changing. We were releasing new models and shipping new features regularly, which made the definition of “correct” a moving target.
Three common sources of “correctness.”
Tests
Tests were the easiest place for us to start, since we already had an existing set of about 700 integration tests. However, two problems limited our ability to trust them to verify the correctness of a migration as high stakes as this (Figure 4).
The tests were coupled to the Python implementation.
An integration test sends a request, then checks the reply and what was sent to other services. Our tests ran the Python API inside the test’s process and mocked services, like billing and rate limiting, in Python’s memory. The tests had to change along with the code, and Claude helped with both. Now, a “pass” could mean that the code was right, or that the test had been changed in a way that let wrong code through. We saw this happen: when we audited the ported tests, we found more than 100 weakened assertions.
The tests were incomplete.
The Messages API has dozens of features, and there are far too many configurations to test them exhaustively. Just 20 binary options make over a million combinations—that translates to 12 days of tests at a second each, for one model, before we even vary the prompts inside them. In practice, engineers test a subset that tries to approximate production, but that process inevitably misses cases. Some projects, like Bun, have an independent suite that’s extensive enough to judge a rewrite. Many production services don’t; what counts as correct depends as much on how they behave as on what’s in their tests or documentation.
A ported test may check less than the original (dashed), and tests cover only the combinations someone thought of.
Detecting parity with production
Production data is sometimes “
the only true test
” that new code behaves like the old code. Running requests through old and new code and comparing the results is often called
shadowing
. To understand what we needed to compare, it helps to walk through what happens to a single request on the Messages API (Figure 5). The API validates each request, converts it into a prompt a model can read (the prompt for inference), tokenizes it, and runs it through safety classifiers. A model then writes a reply, one token at a time. On the output side, the API sorts those tokens into text, thinking, and tool calls, streams them to the customer, and counts usage for limits and billing.
The Messages API’s input and output paths. Filled dots are examples of differences we found between Python and Rust. The hollow dot is a risk we had to prevent.
The migration covered both the input and output paths. Some differences were obvious, such as when the Rust API rejected a request that Python had accepted. But many were subtle. For instance, if the Rust API left out part of a prompt, the request would still succeed and the model would still answer, though sometimes with minor differences.
Our Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic (Figure 6). The gap came partly from cases in production traffic that our tests didn’t cover. For example, when Python writes JSON tool calls, it escapes certain characters (e.g., an emoji) by replacing them with text codes. Rust wrote those characters as is, so the two prompts differed by a few bytes. Production also weighted bugs differently. In a test suite, each case counts once, but in live traffic, a bug will show up in each request where it’s triggered, which means a single common bug can cause many mismatches.
How often Rust’s input matched Python’s on the requests we compared. Replies were compared separately. Each dot is a day, and the line is a seven-day median. What we compared changed over time, and six misleading days are left out.
Common
tools
for shadowing often assume that a request can safely run twice, or that a service is deterministic. These assumptions didn’t apply in our case. We had to ensure that a request only counted once toward a customer’s limits and bill. In addition, Claude is nondeterministic, meaning that replies
can differ for the same input
(Figure 7). To address this, we ran the model once and replayed the model output to Rust.
With both versions working from the same model output, we still had to compare every stage before and after the model call, and the results had to match exactly. In many systems, bad input causes an error somewhere down the stack. But since Claude accepts almost any prompt, even a small deviation can change its reply without triggering an error. We compared each step before and after the model call, so that we could pin down any deviation that might change what a customer received.
Diff tools often run the old code twice to learn what varies on its own, then ignore it. Claude's replies vary, so those tools would ignore them, along with any bugs in them.
It was important to us to do this in a way that protected user privacy. To do that we had to work without reading user requests or Claude’s replies to them, which means we couldn’t easily see where the Rust and Python versions of the API differed. So instead of looking at text, we recorded the
shape
of each difference, such as where it happened in the service and how big it was. We did this using a few different approaches:
Checkpointing.
Both API versions handle a request using the same steps: accept or reject it, resolve its settings, build the prompt. Every step produces some result, such as an error or the pieces of the prompt, that we could compare step by step, and within the prompt, piece by piece. The first place they differed indicated roughly where the migration code differed from production code (Figure 8).
Comparing at checkpoints, simplified, with made-up values. The first step to differ shows where to look. The record gives the piece, the lengths, and where they first differ, but not the text.
Fingerprint.
Once we knew roughly where each diff resided, we still needed a way to distinguish one bug from another. We recorded where each difference began in the prompt, as well as the length difference between the two versions. Combined with the step and piece of the prompt isolated in checkpointing, we found that bugs presented with a specific fingerprint. That is, one bug tends to leave the same fingerprint on every request it affects (Figure 9). We could then group errors by fingerprint, which helped us triage the fixes.
Fingerprints from one kind of request. A, at the start of the prompt, hid older differences. Once it was fixed, they appeared as B and C. Dots are illustrative.
The result was a shadowing system that produced a small record of each difference between our Rust and Python APIs. Here is an example, with made-up values:
step: build prompt ← where in the code
piece: 2 ← where in the prompt
first diff: byte 17 ← fingerprint
python: 190 bytes ← fingerprint
rust: 190 bytes ← fingerprint
We could then pass this record to an agent to fix it.
Verification loops
Each request that differed left a record in our logs. A single bug could produce hundreds of thousands of nearly identical diff records. Rather than send each to an agent, we ran a script every 10 to 30 minutes that grouped them by which fields differed, then alerted a coordinating Claude agent only when it saw a new
kind
of record. This coordinator assigned a worker agent to own each new kind of record. It also created a new thread in a shared Slack channel where human engineers could follow along and steer it when necessary.
To tackle the many bugs, we set up a series of verification loops. A fast
inner
loop gave agents a sandbox in which they could test ideas and propose fixes. A slower
outer
loop then validated fixes in production. In addition, a
memory loop
recorded any mistakes along the way, saving them so that agents could learn over time (Figure 10).
Verification loops. An edit is checked in a sandbox, and then on shadowed live traffic. People’s corrections become rules. Each loop can catch what the one inside it misses.
Inner loop
When we first started testing this in April, we gave each agent a record that showed where the Rust and Python versions differed. Agents would guess the root cause from the code and open a pull request. Once the fix was reviewed and merged, they deployed it to staging, a preproduction copy of the Rust API where we ran the same shadow comparison on test traffic. The agents checked whether the difference was eliminated. Since every hypothesis needed a review and a deployment, feedback was taking hours or days.
We needed agents to get a signal from verification much sooner, so we moved them into their own workspace. We redesigned the inner loop so that agents could have a place to test ideas quickly and fail safely. Each agent ran in a cloud sandbox with both codebases and fast, local checks for what happens before and after the model call. The input check took a request, built the prompt that each version would send to the model, and showed what differed. Because this check never actually called the model, comparing the versions took under a second. We later added an output check, which ran both versions against a fake model. The output check passed a scripted reply, such as a tool call, through each version and compared the results.
The main limitation was that agents could only see the fingerprint, not the request behind each record. So an agent would hypothesize what had caused the difference, then write its own request or model reply to try to reproduce the difference. Since each agent was writing these itself, it could read both results in full. If the results matched, its guess was wrong and the agent tried again. If they differed the same way the record described, the agent edited the Rust until the two versions matched, then added a test that failed on the old code and passed on the new (Figure 11).
Inner loop. From a fingerprint, an agent guesses the cause and writes a request or reply that should trigger it. Local checks run it through both versions until an edit makes them match.
The seam between the inner and outer loops was a good checkpoint for human review. Inside the sandbox, a wrong guess cost an agent only a few seconds and had no impact on users. Agents could iterate on their own. We allowed a fix to cross into the outer loop only after it had undergone PR review; this allowed engineers to focus their attention on proposed fixes (rather than on guesses) and on the questions the verifiers couldn’t answer, such as whether a difference between the Rust and Python APIs was the result of a bug or a deliberate change.
Agents posted their fixes and evidence to their Slack threads for engineers to review. In mid-May, one of the largest remaining differences between the Rust and Python APIs came from web search. The production API retrieved the web search tool’s description from an internal service. The Rust API didn’t call this service yet, so the tool description was missing from the prompts. An agent proposed a shortcut to copy the text into files that would be readable by Rust. The prompts then matched, and the fix passed the local verifier. But an engineer turned it down because it didn’t solve the problem: Rust would still need to call the service before launch, at which point the workaround would be thrown out (Figure 12).
But the verifier rewarded matching outputs, and the agent found the cheapest way to produce them. A verifier can tell an agent whether the outputs matched, but not whether the fix is good enough to ship. That’s why human review was an important gate.
Agents trace a mismatch to the web search tool across four Slack threads and propose a fix, which an engineer rejects as throwaway code. We shortened and reworded the messages and added the thread names and agent labels.
Outer loop
In the inner loop, agents debugged differences and proposed fixes. At the seam between the inner loop and the outer loop, engineers reviewed the proposed fixes, gave feedback, and approved them to deploy. The outer loop then compared Rust API deployments with and without each fix.
To make that comparison fair, we logged facts about each request we compared, but not its text, including which model and API features it used—for example, prompt caching, tools, or extended thinking. These details let agents compare requests of the same kind (Figure 13) and ask how often the bug’s fingerprint appeared on builds with and without the fix. This way, agents could monitor the new builds for the bug.
Outer loop. An engineer reviews the fix, it deploys, and shadowed traffic shows whether its fingerprint is gone. If not, the task returns to the inner loop.
We designed the outer loop to catch problems that the inner loop missed. The inner loop simulated production quickly but imperfectly: agents could test a hypothesis in seconds, but only on requests they had written, and with a local verifier that wasn’t always configured exactly like production.
This means that sometimes a fix passed in the sandbox and production still showed the difference. The agent assigned to the bug would either see the difference in the new build’s records, or be alerted by the coordinating agent. It then went back to the inner loop and used that evidence to form a new hypothesis.
Memory loop
The inner and outer loops fixed one difference at a time. The
memory
loop improved how agents made those fixes. We didn’t want engineers to have to make the same correction twice, so we recorded what came out of reviews and agents’ own work and applied it to every agent that followed.
For example, when an engineer turned down the web search shortcut (Figure 12), the agent saved a note to memory explaining the decision, the reason for it, and the correct fix, which was to have Rust call the service that supplies tool descriptions.
Building that call took our team weeks, and in the meantime the bug kept producing records. Some had new fingerprints, because the missing text fell at other positions in the prompt or belonged to another tool that used the same service. Agents checked the memory note, recognized the known bug, and linked those records to it, instead of writing another workaround (Figure 14).
Other lessons became general rules for porting and writing Rust. After one agent guessed at Python’s behavior, an engineer made it a rule to port exactly what Python did. An agent then compared the existing code with that rule and found seven more places where the port had relied on a guess.
In June, an agent also went through about 60 of the team’s review comments, grouped the recurring problems and proposed rules, which an engineer edited and approved for
CLAUDE.md
(Figure 14).
The memory loop also encoded some lessons in permanent checks. This included new tests that failed when Rust drifted from Python, lints that banned patterns reviewers kept flagging, and later a merge check that required anyone changing the Python code to make a matching change in Rust or request an exemption.
Memory loop. An engineer’s correction becomes three things: a rule that each new agent reads, a search for the same mistake, and a test.
Looking ahead
It’s increasingly feasible to migrate production systems with Claude, either for better performance or security, without taking an API offline or slowing feature development. Now that the hard part is no longer writing new code, we need to build sufficient confidence that the new system behaves like the old one.
The usual approach to migration is a bit like rebuilding the Ship of Theseus, in which the old ship was replaced plank by plank. Generally it’s been possible to replace planks while the ship still sails, but changing too many planks at once requires coming into dock. To fully stretch the metaphor, Claude now makes it possible to build an identically functioning ship alongside the first—even as the first keeps sailing and having its planks replaced. Agents kept the new ship in step as the old one changed, and we kept checking that the two behaved the same. Once we trusted that they did, we moved the passengers over a few at a time. The new ship sails faster and more efficiently than the old one.
Lessons learned
Verification is the new bottleneck.
Previously, large software projects like migrations were hard to justify because they took too much effort and carried too much risk. But if writing code is no longer the bottleneck, the main constraint becomes how quickly you can verify results. In general, ambition can be increased as long as there’s a way for Claude to verify correctness.
Verification is how you earn confidence.
In math, we use a proof assistant to verify that each step of a proof Claude wrote is valid. For software, tests or
formal verification
can help us gain similar confidence. But when these checks aren’t enough, a production system itself can also be a verifier.
Carefully design the verification signal.
A verifier provides a signal that Claude can act on. We can calibrate this signal to show Claude where things went wrong. Where a proof assistant points to the failing step or a test names the failing case, a production system often offers no such signal by default. Much of our effort for this project went to building such a signal. In this case, checkpoints located each difference
in the code
and fingerprints helped
tell one bug from another
.
Build loops that let Claude autonomously act on the signal.
Our inner loop was fast and ran locally in a sandbox. Agents tested hypotheses in seconds using requests they wrote themselves. The outer loop was slower and checked fixes on shadowed production traffic. The outermost loop was just prose, with corrections saved as rules in memory that could be read by every agent later in the process. Together, these loops allowed us to migrate the Messages API to Rust, which uses about 70% less CPU per request and reduces median time to first token by about 20% (Figure 15).
CPU and memory used per request, and median time to first token, as requests moved from Python (gray) to Rust (blue). Lines are seven-day averages, 100 is about the level just before the move, and each arrow shows the change from the first dot to the second. CPU is one region, memory is all of production, and time to first token is customers' Claude Code requests over a shorter period. In the third panel, the fall before the first dot came while almost all of those requests were still on Python.
Keep the loops simple, so they scale with Claude’s capability.
We tried to put human judgment only into what counted as correct; otherwise we left it up to Claude how to get there. Agents chose which hypotheses to test, how to reproduce each bug, and how to fix it. The verifiers judged the result. Simple loops around strong verifiers allowed us to move productively over time (Figure 16).
Changes merged to our API's Rust code in each two-week period, from April until public traffic moved to Rust in September 2026. Not all of them are migration work.
Move toward outer loops.
At first, we had our engineers working inside the inner loop, running Claude and chasing differences themselves. Later, they moved to the seam between loops, helping to steer agents and reviewing fixes in Slack. But as the system matured, they increasingly moved to the edge, where they could provide the highest leverage, writing the rules and checks that agents worked within. As Claude grew more intelligent (and as we grew more intelligent at working with it), we evolved from directing Claude to Claude directing itself, relying on humans mainly for important judgment calls.

items.content:
Multi-turn AI apps with external state commonly hit the same snag: ledger balances and itineraries shift with every turn, and pending cards or language settings can change at any time. Rewriting
system
or rebuilding history repeatedly invalidates the KV cache. Relying solely on incremental diffs is equally fragile: over dozens of turns, the model begins dropping earlier entries.
Travel assistant app
Nyatabi
's V2 message assembly and memory design (built on DeepSeek
deepseek-flash
and default-enabled
thinking
) offers a production-tested solution verified under live load. Over a three-day travel ledger conversation (20 turns, 34 calls, and 6 web searches), this architecture achieved an overall cache hit rate of 96.2% (97.0% excluding cold starts, with a median of 97.7% per call), tallying 376,064 cached read tokens against only 14,816 misses and zero prefix breaks.
The first two sections break down append-only prefixes and periodic full-section refreshes for dynamic state. The last two explore
thinking
toggle consistency during compaction, as well as a layered memory architecture that replaces main-conversation memory tools with a lightweight classifier.
Nyatabi — your AI travel companion for iPhone
Plan with Musubi, explore together, split spending fairly and turn your route into memories. Your whole journey, in one local-first iPhone app.
Nyatabi
Append-Only Prefixes: Moving Clock and User Context Out of System
Achieving high cache hits rests on a simple principle: previously sent bytes must never change. Each request sent to the model simply extends the prior request's bytes with a few new messages at the end. When external state changes, you append only the delta or an update block, relying on rules in
system
to treat the latest version as authoritative.
Time handling is the first common source of cache breakage. Many systems inject the current clock into
system
, changing the prefix every minute. Nyatabi eliminated the global clock section entirely. Instead, request assembly prepends a
<sent_at>2027-01-10 Sun 12:10 +09:00</sent_at>
tag to every user message during request assembly, leaving database storage and client UI untouched. 'Today' or 'Day N of the trip' is derived by the model from the most recent
<sent_at>
tag. Embedding the UTC offset directly in every message also pays off when users travel across time zones: older messages keep their original offsets while new ones record the new zone, sparing the model from having to re-read the session start.
Language and time zone settings likewise cannot live in
system
or in session-level
configurationKey
. Request payloads are organized from top to bottom into eight layers by byte stability; the diagram below shows which changes require starting a new session and which can simply be appended at the end.
Whiteboard
Working down this hierarchy, only changes in layers 1–2 warrant a new session (such as switching scenarios, toggling web search, or switching between ledgers with and without reference chats).
<user_context>
is sent as the very first
user
message of the session. When a user switches their phone language from Chinese to English mid-conversation, the existing prefix stays unchanged. Only a short
<user_context_update>
block appended at the end. That adds only 427 characters to the entire turn, and the cache continues to hit.
Taking the 20-turn live Okinawa ledger test as an example, the Turn 1 cold-start request payload JSON measured 16,328 characters (
system
with 6,727 characters plus 6 tools). The second model call after tool execution did not resend ledger state; it only appended
tool_use
and
tool_result
, adding just 366 characters. Amounts and exchange rates use plain numbers with currency codes instead of locale-formatted strings, preventing localization formatting variations from creating meaningless diffs.
Dynamic State Sync: Why Pure Deltas and Resending Full Sections Both Fail in Long Conversations
In an append-only architecture, syncing ledger changes to the model cannot follow a single rule. This delta-based approach has an obvious risk: the model's current view of any list is formed by replaying multiple scattered deltas over the initial full section. An amount edit looks like a deletion followed by an addition, and an expense dropping out of the recent-20 window also looks like a deletion. In a long conversation, could the model lose track of this chain of updates?
Our first round of online evaluations ran for 40 dialogue turns (with conversations running up to ~30K tokens across 3 random seeds and 24 checkpoints), continuously changing expenses and itineraries out-of-band while updating pending confirmation cards. The delta group clearly beat full resends: both tied on expense totals and items (24/24) and tomorrow's itinerary (23/24), but on pending confirmation cards, the delta group scored 24/24 while full resends managed only 14/24. Total input tokens also favored deltas: 520K versus 900K (15K vs. 38K misses).
Extending the test to 60 turns with 300-word responses and up to 6,000-character tool outputs from
read_reference_conversation
(pushing history past 96KB and triggering mid-run compaction, across 3 seeds with 36 checkpoints) completely reversed the picture. Both pure deltas and full resends failed on pending confirmation cards; only periodic full refreshes remained stable.

Comparing the two series in the bar chart reveals two entirely different failure modes. In the baseline run, the delta-only approach dropped to 20/36, failing in an identical way every time: the model reported only the cards in the most recent
<added>
tag, dropping entries added earlier (in one case reporting only 1 card out of 5).
Resending full sections did even worse in the baseline run, falling to 19/36 and often returning an empty array (
[]
. Digging into the samples showed why: sending the full section caused the model to treat every
<context>
appear to the model like a complete snapshot. If no cards changed in the current turn, the newest
<context>
omitted the
<cards>
sections, the model incorrectly assumes there are currently no pending cards. The comparison data confirms this: when cards changed in the current turn, accuracy was 12/12; when they did not, it plunged to 7/24. Incremental messages tagged with
update="changes"
actually signaled to the model that it needed to scan back through history.
The resulting fix consists of two steps, similar to keyframes in video encoding:
Track counts independently for the three list sections (
expenses
/

/

). Once 4 incremental updates accumulate since the last full section, or the appended messages and tool context exceed 16K characters, send the update as a full section instead, then resume sending deltas.
Add an explicit rule to
system
:
A section missing from the latest <context> has not changed; its last version still applies.
A 60-turn retest with this prompt rule confirmed the diagnosis: pending card accuracy for the full-resend group jumped from 19/36 to 34/36. Our production strategy—sending a full refresh every 4 updates or 16KB—virtually matched full resends across the board: 36/36 on today's expenses and totals, 36/36 on tomorrow's itinerary, and 33/36 on pending cards. Total input came to 4.37M tokens—only 6% more than pure deltas (4.14M), and 26% less than resending full sections every turn (5.89M).
Cache Constraints of History Compaction and the Thinking Toggle Trap
As conversations grow longer, history compaction must also follow the append-only rule. Before each turn starts (on new user messages and only once past three user messages), compaction triggers if either condition is met: the prior request's token count, excluding web searches, reaches 160,000—which is 80% of
min(20 万, 模型窗口)
(while
deepseek-flash
has a 1M window, capping it at 200K guarantees the compaction request fits in one shot without chunking). If tokens remain below that threshold, compaction also triggers when message history reaches 96KB, or hits 24KB after 30 minutes of idle time.
When performing compaction, the server takes the exact snapshot of the current session's previous request (covering
system
, tool definitions, and all historical messages and context), appends any subsequent new messages excluding the current turn's query, and appends a single
<compaction_request>
tag at the very end. The prompt uses the
<sent_at>
of the third-to-last user message as a boundary, requiring the summary to cover everything prior (up to 8,000 characters) while keeping the last 3 turns verbatim from that boundary onward. The prompt also forbids recording pending or ignored card states (which are deferred to
<cards>
), forbids repeating ledger details and itineraries from
<context>
, forbids misrepresenting assistant suggestions as user agreements, and disallows tool calls.
A new session starts by assembling context in this exact order: current values of
<user_context>
→
<history_summary>
→ the latest complete block of
<context>
→ the last 3 turns verbatim → the current turn's user message. Placing the latest
<context>
block ahead of older, uncompacted turns slightly disrupts chronological order, but this trade-off anchors the more stable prefix at the very front so subsequent turns hit the cache more easily.

Reusing the existing prefix allowed the compaction request to hit 94% cache reuse, generating 1,180 tokens (including roughly 850 characters of reasoning) in 5.3 seconds. In the new session, the first post-compaction request still shared 72% of its bytes with the previous call (
system
and tools hit the cache directly), and the second request immediately returned to 97%. The summary also preserved cross-turn constraints like 'Xiao Zhou is allergic to peanuts.'
The sneakiest trap in compaction tuning lies in the
thinking
toggle. If you disable thinking mode on compaction calls to trim output costs, the cache instantly breaks. Comparing four test groups against the same ~4,900-token prefix (
system
plus 6 tools), where the second call only appended one message while toggling the switch, yielded these live results:

The chart shows that flipping the switch in either direction caused cached reads to collapse from nearly 5,000 tokens to roughly 1,280, forcing the model to recompute over 3,700 tokens of prefix. Throughout a session, the
thinking
toggle must stay consistent. Compaction calls inherit the main conversation's setting (DeepSeek defaults to thinking enabled), keeping the output cap at 32,768 tokens (180s timeout) so the reasoning trace does not crowd out the summary. Thinking is explicitly turned off only for background memory workers that share no prefix and carry no tools.
On-Demand Mounting and Lookback for Reference Conversations
For ledgers created from the home screen conversation,
<overview>
includes only an excerpt of the most recent 1,500 characters from that initial conversation (truncated at message boundaries). When constraints mentioned earlier (such as 'Xiao Zhou is allergic to peanuts') fall outside the excerpt, the model pages backward from newest to oldest using the read-only tool
read_reference_conversation
. Each page returns at most 20 messages and 6,000 characters, using
earlier_before
pagination that caps results to messages sent before the ledger was created. This tool is mounted only when a ledger actually references a conversation, preventing accidental calls on standalone ledgers while keeping the tool definitions constant throughout the session.
Home Screen Chat and Stateless Form Assistant
The same prefix-isolation model extends to two other lightweight entry points. In the home screen chat, the
system
prompt shrinks to 2,181 characters, and its context contains only a freshly resent full
<home>
section. The form assistant for creating ledgers and itineraries skips the context pipeline altogether, maintaining no sessions or snapshots and having the client pass the full history on each turn. It also places
<user_context>
in the first
user
message. Each subsequent user message combines
<sent_at>
, the current form JSON (
<form>
, supporting manual user edits), and the raw input. Turn 2 adds only 347 characters.
Tool-Free Layered Memory: Jev Routing and Background LLM Operators
Most agents implement memory through read and write tools called by the primary model. That expands the tool schema, slows down real-time replies, and frequently causes missed lookups or incorrect saves. Nyatabi's Memory v2 discards memory tools from the main chat. Instead, every user message runs through Jev, a lightweight classifier (
jev-latest
, taking ~250ms concurrently with context assembly, with an 800ms timeout). Jev synchronously determines on-demand recall, while background jobs handle writes asynchronously.
In the main chat, the memories visible to the model are separated into three tiers by lifecycle and privacy scope, integrating cleanly into the append-only pipeline:

The injection layer guards three filtering boundaries: memories created in the current session are excluded because their raw text is already in the history; expired short-term memories (7, 30, or 90 days) are dropped; and inferred memories (
inferred

source="inferred"
with 'prefers quiet accommodations', the model replied, 'If you want somewhere quieter, the latter two areas would suit you better,' rather than claiming, 'You've always liked quiet places.'
Member privacy boundaries are also enforced at the injection layer. When Kobayashi noted in a shared ledger, 'I don't eat beef, and neither does Alice. Also, don't schedule early morning itineraries,' the system saved his beef restriction as a persistent user trait, 'no early mornings' as his personal itinerary preference for this ledger, and Alice's beef restriction as a shared member trait. When Bob later asked for dinner recommendations in that same ledger, his
<memory>
block included only Alice's dietary restrictions, keeping Kobayashi's two notes completely isolated.
The complete synchronous recall and 5-step background write pipeline is structured as follows:
Reading this diagram comes down to the two branches. The upper synchronous path handles low-latency recall alone, protecting time-to-first-token. The lower asynchronous path runs background workers only after the main turn finishes, letting the classifier resolve whether to save, for whom, in what category, and for how long, leaving only a narrow text-editing step for the LLM.
The Operator Receives All Visible Memories for the Subject
When assembling the
existing

(0.89), so

["self"]

<user_context_update>
purged the obsolete restriction before the next turn.
Tool-Free Operator with Dual Code Validation
The background operator (
deepseek-flash
,

,

disabled, static system prompt with
cache_control
) runs for just one turn and returns a single
{"ops":[...]}
object (supporting

/

/

/

, up to 5 operations). Omitting tool definitions eliminates schema overhead on every request, with field validity verified twice in code: first when parsing the operator's response, and again before writing to database storage.
Validation rules are kept exceptionally strict:
evidence
must be a contiguous substring of
userText
to prevent the model from citing assistant replies or inventing statements.
(subject, feature)
must fall within the
routed
list produced in step 3.

and
source
come directly from Jev, ignoring any LLM inference. Trip-specific memories from home screen chats are dropped since there is no ledger to bind them to. Across two live sessions and evaluations spanning 11 calls in all, every response was valid JSON.
7-Turn Live Costs and False-Positive Overhead
Across seven real-world integration turns testing member isolation, cross-session home chats, and restriction revocations, costs broke down as follows:

Jev consumed an average of about 1,570 tokens per turn (700–900 tokens on the first synchronous pass). Even when a false positive occurred—such as scoring 'Let's pick another place' at 0.75 for involving Alice—running the remaining steps through the operator required only about 2,000 Jev tokens plus a brief call returning an empty array (
{"ops":[]}
). On the dedicated memory eval suite, all expected on-demand traits triggered across 14 routing tests (with 7 over-triggers that merely injected existing memories), subject attribution matched in 12 of 14 cases, and background writes were accurate in 5 out of 5.
Remaining Gaps and Known Limitations
Across 20 turns of online cache stress testing, hit rates held steady at 98–99% as prefixes lengthened. Excluding the three calls right after web searches, cache misses averaged just 247 tokens per turn. The three lowest dips (85.5%, 90.7%, and 89.6%) all followed web searches, where the model generated lengthy replies from fresh search results that naturally introduced uncacheable tokens. Because DeepSeek caches in 128-token blocks, every call also incurs an alignment rounding loss of up to 127 tokens.
As of this baseline release—with all multi-client and server regression suites passing—the test logs show three known limitations still in place:
thinking
is enabled, compaction summaries occasionally weave in expenses and plans from
<context>
, or repeat parts of the conversation already kept verbatim past the cutoff point. This adds a few hundred characters of duplication without affecting correctness.
In its second pass, Jev occasionally routes a statement into multiple categories (for instance, 'I don't eat beef, and neither does Alice' triggers both allergies and dietary restrictions). The system currently relies on the LLM operator rule that only writes entries backed by verbatim text; across seven live turns and five eval cases, it made zero incorrect writes.
On-demand recall triggers run slightly broad: questions about transit or attractions often pull in pace and planning preferences as well. The only side effect is injecting extra existing memories, with no missed recalls observed so far.

items.title: Vulnerability Analysis CVE-2026-129243 GeoServer Service Security Bypass via Prefixed Service
items.content:
Introduction
GeoServer is a widely adopted open-source server written in Java that enables organizations, researchers, and developers to view, share, and edit geospatial data using open standards established by the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC). Because GeoServer deployments frequently expose sensitive spatial datasets, administrative workflows, and transactional endpoints across public or enterprise networks, administrators rely heavily on granular service-level access controls to restrict high-risk operations—such as Web Feature Service (WFS) transactions, stored query creation, or restricted map queries—exclusively to authenticated and authorized user roles.
CVE-2026-129243
(tracked internally by the GeoServer project as
GEOS-12284
) is a high-severity authorization bypass vulnerability affecting core GeoServer components. Assigned a CVSS score of
8.8
, the flaw allows unauthenticated or unauthorized attackers to circumvent configured service security rules simply by prepending an arbitrary prefix to a service name (for example, submitting
x/WFS
instead of
WFS
). Following its public disclosure in GeoServer’s November 2026 security update, threat intelligence researchers at watchTowr observed active reconnaissance and error-based exploitation probes targeting internet-facing GeoServer instances, highlighting the urgency of immediate remediation and defensive hardening across production geospatial infrastructure. When chained with secondary flaws, this bypass can escalate privileges from anonymous access to full remote code execution.
Learning
Objectives
By reading this analysis, security engineers, penetration testers, and GIS administrators will be able to:
Understand the root cause of
CVE-2026-129243
and how authorization mismatches occur between request dispatching and service-security rule evaluation.
Identify how prefixed service identifiers (such as
x/WFS
) bypass service-level access restrictions in GeoServer’s core OGC Web Services (OWS) architecture.
Determine which GeoServer release branches and core artifacts are affected and identify the patched versions required for remediation.
Apply effective upgrade and defense-in-depth mitigation strategies to protect internet-facing GeoServer deployments.
What is GeoServer Service Security Bypass via Prefixed Service (CVE-2026-129243)
CVE-2026-129243 is an improper authorization vulnerability within GeoServer’s core OGC Web Services request-handling framework. GeoServer exposes spatial capabilities through standardized OGC protocols—including Web Map Service (WMS), Web Feature Service (WFS), Web Coverage Service (WCS), and Web Processing Service (WPS)—which frequently handle sensitive data modification and server-side processing tasks. To secure these endpoints, GeoServer administrators configure service-level access control rules (typically defined in
services.properties
or managed via security extensions such as GeoFence). These rules map specific services and operations to required user roles—for example, permitting anonymous read queries via
wfs.GetFeature
while restricting state-changing or administrative operations like
wfs.Transaction
or stored query creation exclusively to administrative accounts. CVE-2026-129243 breaks this security boundary due to a discrepancy between service dispatch resolution and service-security rule matching. When an attacker prepends a prefix to a service identifier—such as
x/WFS
—the security subsystem fails to associate the prefixed string with the protected
WFS
access rules, while the underlying OWS dispatcher still resolves and executes the target
WFS
operation. Security researchers at watchTowr demonstrated that attackers can leverage this flaw to bypass admin-only restrictions on creating WFS stored queries and chain the access with XML parsing vulnerabilities to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution.
Service-Level Rule Evasion:
Prefixed service identifiers such as
x/WFS
fail to match explicit role restrictions defined for canonical service names like
wfs
in GeoServer’s security configuration.
Unauthorized OWS Execution:
Unauthenticated or low-privileged users can invoke restricted OWS operations—including administrative stored query creation or transactional edits—that were explicitly locked down.
High-Impact Exploit Chaining:
Bypassing service-level security rules provides a critical initial foothold that can be chained with secondary vulnerabilities (such as
CVE-2026-129245
) to achieve full remote code execution.
Active Exploitation Probing:
Automated scanning campaigns have been observed sending error-based probes with prefixed service parameters to identify vulnerable GeoServer hosts on the public internet.
flowchart TD
A[Incoming OGC Request] --> B{Service Parameter Format}
B -->|Standard: service=WFS| C[Security Rule Matcher]
C --> D[Matches rule: wfs.* = ROLE_ADMIN]
D --> E[Access Denied: HTTP 403 Forbidden]
B -->|Prefixed: service=x/WFS| F[Security Rule Matcher]
F --> G[No rule found for 'x/WFS' -> Fallback to Anonymous]
G --> H[OWS Dispatcher Normalizes 'x/WFS' -> 'WFS']
H --> I[Executes Restricted WFS Operation: HTTP 200 OK]
Technical Detail: How the Vulnerability Works
In GeoServer’s request-processing pipeline, incoming OGC Web Services requests pass through two distinct stages before any geospatial data or administrative action is executed. First, a security enforcement layer intercepts the request and inspects the requested service and operation parameters against the active service access control list. Second, once authorized, the request is handed off to the OWS
Dispatcher
, which resolves the target service bean and invokes the requested operation. The vulnerability arises because these two stages normalize and interpret the
service
parameter differently when a path-like prefix is introduced. During the authorization check, the security rule evaluator performs a lookup using the raw, unstripped service string (
x/WFS
). Because administrators configure rules against canonical service names (for example,
wfs.CreateStoredQuery=ROLE_ADMINISTRATOR
), the lookup finds no matching restriction for
x/WFS
and defaults to permitting the request under anonymous permissions.
Once the security check passes, the OWS dispatcher processes the same
x/WFS
parameter using routing logic that splits or strips the leading prefix segment before the slash delimiter. As a result, the dispatcher resolves the trailing
WFS
identifier to the legitimate Web Feature Service handler and executes the privileged operation without authentication. Threat actors have also leveraged malformed or prefixed service probes to trigger predictable server error responses, allowing them to remotely fingerprint unpatched instances before launching full exploit payloads.
Unnormalized Security Lookup:
The service-security filter evaluates
x/WFS
literally against configured access control entries, missing rules bound to
wfs
.
Permissive Default Fallback:
When no explicit rule matches the prefixed service identifier, GeoServer’s authorization layer falls back to default anonymous access rather than rejecting the malformed service name.
Prefix Stripping in OWS Dispatch:
Downstream dispatch resolution extracts the trailing
WFS
token after the slash character and maps it directly to the active WFS service descriptor.
Error-Based Fingerprinting:
Attackers send crafted requests containing prefixed or malformed service identifiers to analyze exception messages and confirm whether a target server is vulnerable.
Affected Software & Plugins
CVE-2026-129243 resides in GeoServer’s core OGC Web Services and main application modules (
org.geoserver:gs-ows
and
org.geoserver:gs-main
). Because the flaw is embedded in core request dispatching and security evaluation logic rather than an optional extension, all standard GeoServer deployments running unpatched releases across the
2.27.x
,
2.28.x
, and
3.0.x
branches are affected. The GeoServer project addressed this vulnerability in its security release updates by aligning service identifier normalization between the security subsystem and the OWS dispatcher. Administrators running external authorization plugins—such as
GeoFence
or custom Access Control List (ACL) modules—should ensure that both the core GeoServer installation and any accompanying security extensions are upgraded to the matching patched release line.
GeoServer 3.0.x Branch:
Versions
3.0.0
through
3.0.1
are vulnerable; remediated in
GeoServer 3.0.2
.
GeoServer 2.28.x Branch:
Versions
2.28.0
through
2.28.5
are vulnerable; remediated in
GeoServer 2.28.6
.
GeoServer 2.27.x Branch:
Versions up to
2.27.6
are vulnerable; remediated in
GeoServer 2.27.7
.
Core Artifacts & Security Plugins:
Directly affects core
org.geoserver:gs-ows
and
org.geoserver:gs-main
components; environments utilizing
GeoFence
or external ACL plugins must verify compatibility with the patched
3.0.2
,
2.28.6
, or
2.27.7
builds.
Conclusion
CVE-2026-129243 illustrates how subtle parsing inconsistencies between security enforcement filters and application-level dispatchers can render granular access controls ineffective. By prepending a simple prefix such as
x/WFS
to a service parameter, an unauthenticated attacker can sidestep role-based restrictions and invoke privileged OGC operations on unpatched GeoServer deployments. The real-world risk posed by this vulnerability is heightened by confirmed active reconnaissance from threat actors and the documented ability to chain this authorization bypass with WFS stored query flaws to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. Organizations exposing GeoServer instances to external networks must treat this flaw as a critical remediation priority. Administrators should immediately upgrade affected deployments to
GeoServer 3.0.2
,
2.28.6
, or
2.27.7
. As an interim defense-in-depth measure where immediate patching is not feasible, security teams should configure Web Application Firewall (WAF) or reverse-proxy rules to reject any request whose
service
query parameter contains a slash (
/
) or deviates from strict alphanumeric OGC service names (
WMS
,
WFS
,
WCS
,
WPS
), and disable any unused transactional or stored query capabilities.

items.title: 5 美元一次的 AI 黑客来了，小项目太小所以安全的时代结束了
items.content:
做个人项目、独立产品或者小团队业务，大家往往都有一种心理安慰：我只是一个小网站，没什么用户隐私，账上也没多少钱，黑客费尽心机来搞我有什么用呢？
过去十几年来，这层心理防线在多数情况下确实有用。安全圈管这叫靠渺小隐身。以前发动一次有针对性的入侵，需要熟练的黑客花几天踩点、读代码、写脚本，人力摆在那，打一个没有油水的小网站连人工费都赚不回来。大公司才是重点目标，小项目只要不把数据库密码设成
123456，多数能平安度日。
但 2026
年秋天，几家安全公司发现了一批黑客忘了设密码的攻击后台，暴露了一个现实：这层隐身护甲已经破了。黑客用开源
AI 工具，把一次自动入侵的成本拉到了 5 到 25
美元，就算你的网站本身一文不值，你服务器里的 AI
密钥和本地算力，现在本身就是可以直接变现的通用货币。
为什么 5
美元一次的草台班子，专打以前没人碰的小目标
要想理解为什么小项目不再安全，得先看看今天的 AI
攻击工具长什么样。
在过去的半年中，GitHub 上出现了大约 45 个开源的 AI
自动化渗透测试工具，其中最流行的是 ARTEX、Cairn 和
PentAGI，排名前五的几款合计拿到了 6
万多个星标。这些工具将上百种传统黑客工具集成起来，形成面向大模型的接口。只要提供一个目标网址，它们就会启动多个子代理自动进行扫描、发现漏洞、编写代码并尝试入侵。ARTEX
的作者在 10 月初下架了 GitHub 仓库，但当时已经有 12,000
多个分支，下架挡不住扩散。美国联邦调查局在 11 月 13 日的
专项通报
中提到，仅公网暴露的
ARTEX 控制台就有 1,600 多个。
这些工具真的有那么厉害吗？并不。安全机构 NorForge 分析了 20
多个黑客自己忘了设密码的 Cairn 面板，覆盖了 1,100 多个实际攻击项目，在
调查报告
里给出了真实的命中率：平均成功率只有大约
10%，就算攻进去了，平均也要折腾将近 23 个小时。
真实后台日志里到处都是草台班子式的翻车现场。云安全公司 Wiz 在
追踪分析
中看到，ARTEX
两分钟内对着微软高度加固的登录接口连发 60
多次没有数字签名的假凭证，就像拿没盖章的假门禁卡连刷 60
次。更离谱的是另一家机构 Gambit Security 在
调查
里记录的事故：黑客用三款开源工具
5 天扫描 105 家在线商业站点，攻破至少 27 家公司并偷走 60
多万条未过期信用卡记录；可是在入侵一家自行车零售商后，AI
代理执行清理脚本时通配符写得太宽，顺手把受害者数据库里的 180
张表连带备份表全删光了。甚至连黑客自己的运维都一塌糊涂，不少暴露面板压根没设密码，反遭同行劫持偷走密钥。
Wiz
直接指出，这些工具没有发明任何新技术，能打进来的目标全靠弱口令、泄露密钥、没打补丁的旧插件这类老缺口。
那为什么这种粗糙、成功率只有 10%
的攻击，反而让小团队更危险？算一笔账就明白了：NorForge
测算出，用低价模型跑一次 Cairn 的自动化攻击，平均成本只要约 5
美元；Gambit 统计攻破 27 家公司的后台，平均每个目标只需 25.46
美元的扫描和攻击成本。过去雇熟练黑客盯一个中小网站按天计酬，划不来就不干；现在把单次尝试的价格压到一顿快餐钱，机器可以
24 小时不眠不休地撒网。对黑客来说，完全不需要每次都成功，只要每扫 10
家能撞中 1
家，这门生意就能稳定赚钱。小网站以前赖以生存的门槛，就这样被一顿快餐钱抹平了。
小项目的隐身护盾如何消失：人工黑客按天计费只盯大目标，而
5 美元 AI 自动化流水线靠 10% 成功率即可 24 小时批量扫网盈利
你的项目没油水，但你的
API 密钥能直接养活攻击机
看到这里，很多个人开发者会想：我只是做个技术博客、开源演示站或内部小工具，没信用卡没付费用户，黑客花
5 美元攻进来能捞什么？
答案就在你的环境变量和本地服务里。2026 年，大模型的算力和 API
额度本身就成了黑客最爱抢的资产。
Google 在 11 月的
专项追踪报告
里披露，盗刷云端大模型额度已经发展成成熟的地下黑产。黑客只要通过泄露密钥或钓鱼拿到一个云账号，就会立刻开启大模型接口或租用高端显卡，一天能刷出超过
10 万美元账单，最严重的案例在受害者察觉前累计损失达到 100
万美元。这些偷来的额度会流向地下中转站，有的平台甚至以每月 60
美元兜售所谓无限量前沿模型套餐。
2026
年夏天以后，黑客把偷来的算力不仅倒卖换钱，还会直接拿来喂给自家的攻击代理。6
月，安全公司 Sysdig
首次在真实网络中观察到黑客把公网不设密码的本地模型服务 Ollama
接入自动扫描流程。同年秋天，
亚马逊安全团队用陷阱服务器
抓到
ARTEX 跑通了完整循环：它专门扫描公网暴露的 One API、LiteLLM 和 Ollama
等模型中转服务，把偷来的 API
密钥测完额度后，直接塞进自家配置文件里，用来支付下一轮扫网的账单。
很多开发者图方便，把自己的 Ollama
或中转网关架在测试服务器或家里，端口直接暴露在公网且不带密码，甚至把测试用的
API
密钥扔在公开仓库里。对黑客来说，这等于一台随时能薅羊毛的矿机，哪怕上面一个业务数据都没有。
有人可能会说，这些厂商不是都有内容安全护栏，不会帮别人写攻击性代码吗？但实际上，这种护栏对开源攻击工具来说基本无效。安全公司
Elastic 在 11 月 13 日对其
源码的审计
里分析了五个流行框架，发现没有一个框架会检查用户有没有获得授权，反而内置了规避内容安全护栏的策略，比如
Cairn 碰到某个模型拒答后，会自动等 5
秒换另一个模型继续尝试。联邦调查局的报告也提到，活跃的 ARTEX
实例主要调用的是价格低廉、安全护栏宽松的 DeepSeek Flash
系列。同时，开源大模型在普通笔记本上不到 10
分钟就能移除安全护栏，因此单靠大厂封号和安全护栏已经很难遏制这种以偷养偷的机器。
以偷养偷的自动化攻击闭环：开源攻击框架扫描公网暴露的
AI 网关与云账号，窃取 API 密钥后经地下中转站或直接回灌自身，以 5 到 25
美元的低成本驱动下一轮批量攻击
从装插件到写代码，两个新入口正在贴近普通开发者
即使你把模型服务藏在内网，日常只是建站装开源插件、写代码用 AI
编程助手，2026 年秋天也出现了两个直接贴近日常开发习惯的新变化。
第一个变化是开源软件发布安全补丁后，留给你慢慢升级的时间几乎没有了。以前大家装了一个
WordPress
插件或者开源组件，看到更新提示过一两周有空再升级，觉得黑客没那么快能研究出利用方法。但是
Google 在 11 月 16 日的
季度威胁报告
里提到，他们在一台公网测试服务器上发现了俄语试点程序
exploit_agent
。它持续盯着主流开源网站软件，一旦官方发了补丁，就自动拉取补丁前后代码做对比，让大模型看修补了什么漏洞，自动生成攻击脚本，不经人工介入就去扫描网上还没升级的站点。
当然，没必要过分夸大这个单一程序的作用。它配置文件里的俄语注释自己都标着试点项目，报告里贴出的代码片段也只是一个简单的检查
WordPress 插件 Spectra 里网址是否匹配的示例。云安全联盟的
独立审计
也指出，报告没有公布该程序的成功率。但这条路线在现实世界中已被验证可行：2026
年 8 月底 PaperCut 打印软件公开漏洞，安全公司 GreyNoise 就
记录到
黑客用
OpenAI 的 Codex 编排工具驱动 DeepSeek 模型，从零开始仅用 70
分钟就对比补丁编写了攻击代码，不到 4
小时攻破第一台真实服务器，两天内拿下 395 家机构的 440
个系统。补丁本身正成为自动化扫网的新起点。
第二个变化发生在你每天打开的本地开发环境里。Google
在同一份季度报告里还顺带披露了一起案例：朝鲜黑客组织 MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE
潜入欧美加密机构的内网代码库后，没有去改业务代码，而是悄悄修改了项目里的
.claude/settings.json
。其他同事只要在本地启动 Claude Code
打开仓库，配置里的钩子就会自动触发下载后门木马。这件事目前还只有 Google
单一来源、没有公开完整技术细节，但它最棘手的地方在于完全没利用软件漏洞，靠的就是开发者对仓库配置文件的默认信任。
小团队和个人开发者，今天就能堵上的四个口子
说到底，个人开发者和小团队没办法养一个全天候的安全组，也不必为此焦虑。现在的自动化工具仍然很不成熟，成功率在
10%
左右，主要捡的是基础安全缺陷的漏。花半小时把下面这四个口子堵上，就能拦下大部分
5 美元扫网的机器。
立刻给自建 AI 服务上锁，把所有 API
密钥设好消费上限。检查你租的云主机或内网穿透服务，确认本地的
Ollama、LiteLLM、One API
等中转接口没有不设密码暴露在公网。去大模型厂商后台，给每个 API
密钥设好月度消费上限，尽量用最小权限和短期临时凭证替代长期静态密钥，免得一个测试项目漏网拖出天价算力账单。
把管理后台藏起来，公网入口套一层网页防火墙。PaperCut 那场 70
分钟造出攻击代码的战役里，开启了 Cloudflare
网页防火墙的目标依然直接挡住了攻击。个人和小团队的后台管理面、旧插件接口尽量收进内网或走
VPN
访问；必须露在公网的站点套上一层基础网页防火墙，遇到高危开源组件补丁一时来不及升级，也能先在入口拦住绝大多数按模板扫描的机器。
把仓库中的 AI
工具配置文件当作可执行代码来审查。
.claude/settings.json
、
.cursorrules
等文件现在可以决定 AI
在本地电脑上的行为，审查级别需要与构建脚本一样高。在从陌生开源仓库拉取代码并执行时，不要为了图方便而默认启用全自动批准执行。
最后，为重要数据准备离线或只读备份。传统防黑客主要防的是数据被窃或被勒索，现在多了一种更荒诞的风险：一个笨手笨脚的
AI 代理在清理痕迹时顺手把你 180
张表连带在线备份一起删光。把备份权限和线上数据库隔开，比事后后悔管用得多。
小项目太小所以没人打的时代确实结束了。好消息是，这些全天候扫网的机器只会选最好捏的软柿子，你不用把自己武装成铜墙铁壁，只要比旁边那批裸奔的服务器多上两把锁，5
美元一次的流水线就会自动滑过去找下一个目标。

items.title: Bring Your Own Interpreter - EDR Evasion with LuaJIT, Julia, Node.js, Deno, and Bun
items.content:
I can’t begin to guess as to how many of my carefully crafted PE based loaders got torn apart by a modern EDR solution, and it wasn’t because the payload was bad. It was because the
loader
was, as always, too predictable.
This post is going to go a different direction. What if the loader wasn’t custom at all? What if it was just a trusted, signed PE that can’t just outright be blocked? A binary developers require to run their code, and one that carries a good reputation? That’s the core idea behind
BYOI - Bring Your Own Interpreter
, at least in my mind.
In today’s post, we’ll walk through five interpreters and runtimes, some of which don’t ever get any shoutouts these days, and they should!
LuaJIT, Julia, Node.js, Deno, and Bun
. I’ll demonstrate how each one stages my very rudimentary, calc.exe position-independent shellcode through an
EnumUILanguagesW
callback trap. I’ve also cooked up a couple of bonus scripts, such as a LuaJIT script that walks the IAT to grab an API, and an
NtSetTimer
APC-based script. I’ll cover these more in detail near the end.
Let’s get to it!
The OS Callback Trap ☎️
If you’ve been around offensive Windows for a while, you know the drill:
VirtualAlloc
, copy the shellcode in,
jmp
to it. Simple, effective, and also the exact pattern every EDR is tuned to notice. 😹
The callback trap inverts that picture. Windows gives us APIs where
we
hand the OS a function pointer, and the OS
calls it
for us on its own schedule. One of my favorites for this is
EnumUILanguagesW
from
kernel32.dll
:
HRESULT
EnumUILanguagesW
(
UILanguageEnumProcW
lpUILanguageEnumProc
,
ULONG
dwFlags
,
LANGID
langid
,
LANGID
baseLangid
);
This API enumerates the user interface languages installed on the system, and for
each
one, it invokes the callback we supply. Here’s the beautiful part: that callback is
any
function pointer. It doesn’t receive much scrutiny nor any validation to my knowledge. So the exploit is trivially simple:
Allocate
RWX
memory (Which we will use
VirtualAllocExNuma
to accomplish just that!)
Copy our position-independent shellcode into it
Pass that memory as the
UILanguageEnumProcW
callback
Call
EnumUILanguagesW
The OS walks the installed UI languages, and for the first one, it calls our shellcode
At step 5, the instruction pointer lands in our RWX buffer, but the
caller
isn’t our script. It’s the Windows enumeration machinery in user-mode
ntdll
/
kernel32
, signed Microsoft code, walking a system list. If an EDR is trying to make sense of who called what, the return address it sees is Microsoft’s, not a hand-rolled
jmp
from a loader.
Why do we care? Let’s line up what the EDR
doesn’t
see in the
EnumUILanguagesW
variant:
No injection APIs
— no
CreateRemoteThread
, no
WriteProcessMemory
, no
SetThreadContext
. The shellcode never crosses a process boundary; it lives in the interpreter’s own address space from the moment it’s allocated.
No PE file, ever
— there’s no second image to load and no section table to parse. The only thing on disk is the interpreter.
No direct call site
— our code path never contains an instruction that jumps into the RWX region. The transfer of control is performed by the OS enumeration loop itself.
No PE loader signatures
— all of the public PE loader byte patterns that EDR solutions typically scan for simply don’t exist.
One thing worth noting before we get into the interpreters: the scripts in this post all allocate their shellcode region with
VirtualAllocExNuma
rather than the classic
VirtualAllocEx
. Under the hood it’s the same
NtAllocateVirtualMemory
syscall, but it’s a less-trodden Win32 entry point than
VirtualAllocEx
, which some user-mode hooking schemes key on by API name. Not a magic shield, but I like it because it adds a touch more obscurity into the mix.
The Payload
Pretty basic really. Every script in this post drops the same position-independent, API-resolving payload: a 303-byte
x64
shellcode that opens
calc.exe
. Position-independent means it has
zero hardcoded addresses
. Basically, every function it needs, it finds at runtime by walking the process’s own data structures.
Up first, LuaJIT!
Let’s start with my favorite:
LuaJIT
. If you know anything about it, you know it’s a
JIT
compiler for Lua 5.1. On Windows, it ships as a
single ~500 KB
luajit.exe
with no installer, no dependencies, and no runtime to babysit. That single-file nature is exactly what makes it perfect for BYOI: you’re bringing
one file
.
Installing LuaJIT
Grab the Windows 64-bit source files from
Download source files
. I just went with building from source using Microsoft’s Visual Studio (MSVC). Instructons can be found here:
Install Instructions
Specifically, these instructions for the install:
Building with MSVC
Open a “Visual Studio Command Prompt” (x86, x64 or ARM64), cd to the directory with the source code and run these commands:
cd
src
msvcbuild
Note
:
Check
the
msvcbuild
.bat
file
for
more
options
.
Then
follow
the
installation
instructions
below
.
Now that you have your compiled binaries, go ahead and copy luajit.exe and lua51.dll (built in the src directory) to a newly created directory (any location is ok).

Julia
is a high-performance based, numerical computing language. If you’ve never touched it, Julia is a full programming language with a JIT, a package ecosystem, and…most relevant to us here: a
built-in FFI
via
ccall
. No third-party packages, no native modules to compile. Here’s how it works:
In Julia, a Foreign Function Interface (FFI) is a built-in mechanism that lets Julia code directly call functions and use data from compiled libraries written in other languages; most notably C, C++, and Fortran—with virtually zero overhead.
Because Julia compiles down to native machine code using LLVM, it shares the same low-level memory and CPU architecture as C. Unlike languages such as Python (which often require writing complex “glue code” or C-extensions to bridge the gap), Julia treats C and Fortran libraries as first-class citizens.
How Julia’s FFI Works
Julia uses a built-in macro called @ccall (or the older ccall function) to interact directly with shared libraries (.dll on Windows, .so on Linux, .dylib on macOS).
To make a call, you simply provide:
The function name and library path where the compiled code lives.
The return type mapped to a Julia equivalent (e.g., Cdouble maps to Float64).
The argument types and values being passed in.
This is very useful toward our goal of executing shellcode using low-level C APIs via Julia’s ccall interface to allocate, protect, and invoke raw memory regions directly. 👍

Subtlety 1: the self-installing dependency.
The script will happily
npm install koffi
on its first run if it’s not present. That’s great for a blog demo and
terrible
for fieldcraft — an
npm install
is a network + disk write +
node.exe
child process trifecta that screams “something just happened on this box.” For real operations you pre-stage

Subtlety 2: koffi’s string prototypes.
koffi declares functions as C-style strings (

node.exe
is the reputation king of this list. It’s running in CI pipelines, npm scripts, and dev tooling on half the endpoints in the world. A policy that whitelists

is
not
uncommon, and reputation-based scoring works in our favor.
Everything is in-process: one RWX allocation, one memcpy from

No script-block logging. Node has no default “log every script that runs” telemetry — the script content is only visible via memory scanning, same as Lua and Julia.

Subtlety 1: typed symbol maps.

and

Zero-dependency FFI

no permission flag

--allow-ffi
, nothing to grep for, nothing in the command line that hints at what the script is about to do.
bun.exe
is a single-file, developer-trusted binary with a fast-growing reputation footprint (it’s installed by a lot of modern tooling by default now).
Putting It All Together — Why This Stays Under the Radar
Let’s zoom out and look at what an EDR actually has to work with when one of these runs. The table below compares the four vehicles side by side:

A few things stand out from that table, and a few things I’m being deliberately honest about not claiming:
What we’ve eliminated
(relative to a compiled loader):
The
custom binary
— the single strongest static indicator of a loader. There is no custom hash, no custom section layout, no AI/ML target. The file on disk is a public interpreter with a public reputation.
The
injection telemetry
— no
CreateRemoteThread
, no
WriteProcessMemory
, no cross-process memory writes. All allocation, copy, and execution happen inside the interpreter’s own address space.
The
image-load event
for the payload — there is no PE to load.
The
direct call site
— the transfer of control into RWX memory is performed by OS enumeration/APC machinery, not by our code.
What the EDR can still see
(and should see — this is evasion, not foolproof invisibility 😸):
A process allocating
RWX
memory and then having a callback land in that non-image region. Modern EDRs with memory-protection monitoring (the kind that track RWX allocations and watch for control-flow transfers into them) will have a legitimate, well-motivated signal here.
A parent/child anomaly:
calc.exe
(or whatever the real payload launches) spawning from
luajit.exe
/
julia.exe
/
node.exe
instead of something like
explorer.exe
. That’s a classic behavioral rule and it will fire.
The interpreter process itself doing an allocation that is unusual for its “personality” (a language runtime allocating
PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE
is not normal behavior for
julia.exe
).
The honest framing:
BYOI doesn’t hide the RWX allocation. It hides the
attacker’s fingerprint
around it.
The EDR sees “a trusted developer tool allocated RWX memory and something ran in it” — which is a real signal, but it’s a signal with no custom hash, no known-bad binary, no injection API, and no script-logging telemetry to cross-reference. It forces the defender to make a judgment call about a
reputable
process instead of matching a pattern.
🛡️ For the Defenders 🛡️
One thing worth noting for defenders reading this: the signals are real, and here’s where I’d look, in rough order of effort:
RWX + non-image callback
: alert on
NtAllocateVirtualMemory
with
PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE
followed by a control-flow transfer into that region
that does not originate from a user-mode
call
in the same module
. The return address sitting in
ntdll
/
kernel32
enumeration code is the tell.
--allow-ffi
in command lines
: a one-line grep across process-creation events. Deno FFI usage is
declared
— use that.
npm install
in dev-tool process trees
:
node.exe
spawning
npm install
in a user profile directory, out of band from any editor, is worth a look.
Parent/child anomalies
: Any unusual child process with a parent that’s a scripting runtime.
Unreputable small binaries that
are
interpreters
:
luajit.exe
at 500 KB has far less reputation cushion than
node.exe
. If an unknown small binary is a script interpreter
and
is allocating RWX, that’s two weak signals that reinforce each other.
The counter to all of the above, of course, is that these are all
behavioral
signals against
trusted
processes, which is exactly the tradeoff BYOI makes. You’re trading “obviously bad binary” for “weird behavior from a good binary.”
Full Source Code
All five scripts from this post:

iatenum.lua
— the IAT-assisted resolution variant for LuaJIT.
Grab the full source for: iatenum.lua on Ko-fi
This is the same
EnumUILanguagesW
trick, but with a twist on
how the script finds its own APIs
. Instead of binding
VirtualAllocExNuma
and
EnumUILanguagesW
directly through
ffi.load("kernel32")
, the script walks the
interpreter’s own Import Address Table
at runtime — parsing
luajit.exe

GetModuleHandleA(nil)
, then DOS header →
e_lfanew
→
IMAGE_NT_HEADERS
→ import data directory), printing the full import table x64dbg-style as it goes:
[*] Imports for luajit.exe (base 0x7ff7a1b2c000)
0x00007ff7a1b2c678 Import kernel32.dll.GetModuleHandleA
0x00007ff7a1b2c670 Import kernel32.dll.GetProcAddress
0x00007ff7a1b2c668 Import kernel32.dll.ExitProcess
...
[+] Found kernel32.dll.GetProcAddress
IAT slot: 0x7ff7a1b2c670
Value: 0x7ff9d8e4f1a0
The walk reads the
already-resolved pointer
sitting in each IAT slot. The value the Windows loader wrote there at process start, so there’s no string lookup or export walk happening in the script at all. Once
GetProcAddress
is found, the script
ffi.cast
s that pointer into a function-pointer typedef and uses it to resolve
VirtualAllocExNuma
,
EnumUILanguagesW
,
VirtualFree
, and
GetCurrentProcess
from the
kernel32.dll
module handle at runtime.
The subtle payoff: the script carries
no static FFI binding
to the allocation or enumeration APIs. Those references only exist as resolved pointers in memory after the IAT walk. The one exception is
GetModuleHandleA
itself, which the script binds directly through
ffi.load
as the bootstrap: it’s the chicken-and-egg move. You need one FFI binding to find the function that finds all the others. And the IAT walk works on
any
process that imports
GetProcAddress
, which is to say… pretty much any Windows process. 😆
Bonus Content for Members! (Diamond Tier)

APC-based timer tricks are a
